AB.key_differentiator: Both answer the question, but Plan A's methodology is defensible end-to-end to a fundamental-fund PM while Plan B's stacked IV/Callaway-Sant'Anna/Arellano-Bond machinery is neither buildable nor evaluable by this 30-person shop with one engineer and no production ML.
AB.rationale: The firm is a mid-size fundamental L/S fund with a data team that runs panel/cohort studies, six-to-eighteen-month horizon, and output that must be defensible to a PM asking 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong.' Both plans correctly measure the asked target (DraftKings deposit dollars/activity conditional on Kalshi adoption) rather than a proxy, and both correctly separate deposits from payouts, worry about attrition-vs-churn, and pre-commit placebos. So goal-match is a wash on target definition. The decision turns on firm fit and complexity. Plan A is a clean event-study/matched-cohort design: winsorized OLS on dollars, LPM for retention, Poisson for counts, a placebo battery, partial-identification breakdown, and an explicit pre-trend test with power. Every step is inspectable and defensible to a fundamental PM, and it directly gives 'adopters vs their counterfactual' — exactly the sizing input requested. Plan B is more sophisticated but imports a systematic/econometrics-shop's arsenal: an IV with a constructed affinity instrument on a holdout, Kleibergen-Paap, Arellano-Bond, Callaway-Sant'Anna, Driscoll-Kraay, permutation nulls layered on the mechanical-denominator problem it created for itself by regressing DK on a share whose denominator contains DK. That denominator choice (H1 'within-user rise in Kalshi share cuts DK by more than the mechanical amount') builds in a circularity Plan B then spends multiple stages trying to defend against — machinery generated to fix a self-inflicted specification. This is exactly the reach-for-the-sophisticated-method-first defect: nobody at this shop will build or maintain a validated IV, and the PM cannot gut-check a conclusion resting on it. Plan B does have real virtues Plan A lacks — the sportsbook-launched prediction-market regime break, broker-distributed Kalshi undercount, and net-funding-vs-round-trip point are genuinely sharper economic observations, and it converts deposits to revenue at take rates. But on error asymmetry (concentrated book, position sizing on named companies, Type I dominant) the more demanding plan is warranted only if the firm can actually evaluate its demands, and Plan B's rigor lives in methods the audience cannot audit. Plan A also front-loads its kill test (parallel pre-trends, coverage audit) and is stoppable halfway with something a PM can use. Neither plan invents a P&L number; both stay near the question. I'd staff Plan A and lift Plan B's regime-break and net-funding refinements into it.

AB.key_differentiator: Plan B gates the measurement question — does panel MAU actually track billable seats — before doing any ARR-prediction work, while Plan A jumps straight to fitting MAU→ARR without first establishing the intermediate link the mechanism depends on.
AB.rationale: Both plans are competent, firm-appropriate (fundamental L/S, six-to-eighteen-month horizon, panel data they routinely buy, output that changes named-company sizing and must survive a PM asking what would have to be true to be wrong), and both correctly predict ARR rather than an easier adjacent quantity with proper point-in-time discipline. The question is really about a two-link chain: MAU→seats→ARR. Plan A models MAU→ARR directly and treats price/mix and MAU-per-seat drift as controls or exclusions, so the decisive measurement failure — MAU not tracking billable seats — is diffused across the pitfalls section rather than tested first. Plan B makes exactly that link the gate, on the subset of firms that disclose seats/employees/customers, with a pre-committed kill criterion: if MAU doesn't track seats, you get a negative result and a taxonomy, not a salvage regression. That is the correctly sequenced, entropy-reducing order for this question — the check most likely to kill the idea is at the front. Plan B also does the more honest economic decomposition (Var(g_ARR)=Var(seat)+Var(price)+2Cov published before model results, scoping to names where seats dominate) rather than treating price as a nuisance. On error asymmetry, a concentrated L/S book sizing named positions cannot diversify away a false positive, so Type I dominates and Plan B's tighter pre-registered gating (β in a stated band, β=1 tested, partial correlation floor, leave-one-out stability) is a virtue not a cost here. Neither plan invents a P&L number; both stop at 'not demonstrated.' Plan A is genuinely strong — its consumption-priced-names falsification test is excellent and its break-detection is thorough — but it front-loads sophisticated cointegration/robustness machinery while leaving the does-this-measure-seats question implicit. Plan A's random-split-then-gate-on-rolling-origin sequencing also risks leading with a leaky headline. Plan B's ridge+empirical-Bayes step is slightly more machinery than this audience strictly needs, but it is paired with simple verifiable baselines (damped persistence, consensus surprise regression) the PM can check.
issues_with_winner: Ridge with nested CV plus empirical-Bayes shrinkage is more ML-flavored than a fundamental shop with one engineer will comfortably defend; the simpler pooled FE would likely suffice as the headline

Dense with pre-registered thresholds; risk of the gate being tuned to pass rather than genuinely binding
issues_with_loser: Models MAU→ARR directly without first establishing MAU→seats, so the core measurement risk lives in pitfalls rather than as a front gate

BA.key_differentiator: Plan B keeps the target as the disclosed billed quantity (ARR/subscription revenue) and validates against sell-side dispersion in a way this fundamental fund can defend to a PM, while Plan A reframes the question into a seat-proxy gate that answers an adjacent quantity before it will touch ARR.
BA.rationale: Both are strong, over-built, and both correctly treat MAU-per-seat drift and re-basings as the core threats. AB.key_differentiator: The firm's stated killer is a confident wrong match, and only Plan B enforces the strict separation of panel-derived features from external anchors plus institution-level holdout that makes a precision claim on new institutions credible; Plan A validates cohesion, not correctness.
AB.rationale: Both plans are competent and match the goal (blind identification of anonymized IDs). The decisive question is which controls the error the PM says kills the work: a confident wrong match. Plan B is built exactly around that. Its register split (A=panel inputs, B=anchors used for scoring only, CI failing if an anchor leaks into features) directly prevents the circularity where the thing you're trying to predict quietly informs the fingerprint. Its holdout unit is the institution (leave-one-institution-out, then leave-one-country-out), which is the correct unit when the claim is 'we can identify institutions we haven't seen labeled.' It pre-commits a precision target (95%) with an abstain sink and calibrated thresholds (Venn-Abers/conformal), so the default is UNKNOWN rather than a forced guess — the right posture when Type I is ruinous. It sequences a kill pilot first (Netherlands; if it fails there, stop) and puts negative controls (permuted fingerprints score at chance, phantom IDs must abstain) at the front. Plan A is impressive but its validation machinery (silhouette, Jaccard bootstrap, ARI across windows, permutation null) establishes that clusters are cohesive and stable — not that a named match is correct. Cohesion is not correctness, which Plan A itself concedes in its pitfalls, yet its actual naming still rests on a Hungarian rank-matching heuristic with no external ground-truth validation of names. For a desk that will size real positions on a specific bank's customers, 'these clusters are stable' is not the evidence the PM asked for; 'here is held-out precision on institutions labeled from an independent survey' is. Both are heavy for a three-person data team plus one engineer, but Plan B's abstain-by-default and staged country pilots make it steerable and stoppable; Plan A commits to a large feature/cluster/reconcile pipeline before producing anything a PM can act on. The Sinkhorn/Jonker-Volgenant machinery in B is a real concern for a mid-size fund's explainability, but B pairs it with a simple point-estimate assignment and human-inspectable per-ID candidate sets and reasons for abstention.

Governance/GDPR gate zero is real but could sink the whole effort after anchor licensing costs are incurred
The 40% deposit-volume-identifiable floor per country is asserted as a threshold without derivation
issues_with_loser: Validation proves cluster cohesion and stability, not that any named assignment is correct — the exact error the PM says kills the work
No external ground-truth labels; naming rests on a rank-distance Hungarian heuristic with acceptance margins but no measured precision on held-out institutions

Produces little a PM can act on until the full cluster/reconcile pipeline runs; less adaptive and slower to a first defensible match

BA.key_differentiator: The stated kill-condition is a confident wrong match sizing a position on another bank's customers, and Plan A is built around a per-ID abstain, a precision-at-coverage criterion, and institution-level holdout that directly control that Type I error; Plan B leads with clustering whose cohesion is not correctness and only bolts naming on at the end.
BA.rationale: The question is a capability build — can we identify institutions from anonymized IDs — where the firm has explicitly said the fatal error is a confident wrong match, because the desk then underwrites the wrong bank. That makes Type I precision the whole game, and the right unit of validation the institution, not the customer. Plan A targets exactly this: it fixes an ex-ante criterion (share of deposit volume assigned at >=95% precision on held-out institutions, <40% means the country is not identifiable), abstains per-ID with named reasons, holds out at the institution level (leave-one-institution-out and leave-one-country-out with the gap reported), and separates anchor variables from feature variables with a CI gate so labels cannot leak into the map. It also pre-commits a kill: 'if it fails in the Netherlands, stop' — the concentrated market where identification should be easiest, which is the correct entropy-reducing first pilot. Plan B is a clustering-first design: it asks whether IDs form separated clusters and reads axes as country/charter/model, then escalates to names. Its own best pitfall admission — 'cohesion isn't correctness' — is precisely the disease: unsupervised structure can be strong and stable and still not correspond to institution identity, and B's customer-resample bootstraps (Hennig, ARI over windows, permutation null) all measure stability, not accuracy against ground truth. Naming is a late, thin appendage (Hungarian on rank distance within country-archetype cells) with no held-out precision measurement against real labels. For a desk that dies on a confident wrong match, stability metrics are the wrong evidence standard. Both are heavy; A's machinery is mostly earned by the abstain/calibration requirement, whereas B's three-clustering-reconciliation stack is elaborate for a question that is fundamentally a labeled matching problem. Confidence is moderate because A is genuinely over-engineered and its survey-label N (25-60 per country, sometimes <15) is thin — but A at least names that floor and says below 15 is unvalidatable, and it puts the validating labels and controls at the front.

AB.key_differentiator: Both plans read the firm and the falsification structure correctly, but Plan B puts the cheapest disconfirming checks (release language as-signed, consent solicitation, exposure-to-loss delta, price reaction) first and drops the manufactured cross-sectional comparable study that Plan A builds, which this no-quant desk cannot run and does not need.
AB.rationale: This is a single-name event-driven question for a fundamental desk with no quant staff and no dataset-building capacity, on a weeks-to-months horizon. The correct job is to read the documents, exclude the mundane accounting/refinancing/scheduled-release explanations, and only then reach for the strategic story — and to do it fast enough to trade the catalyst. Both plans understand the alternative-hypothesis structure superbly (H0-a through H0-e / H2/H3) and both correctly note that under H1 the second-source qualification must PRECEDE the guarantor exit given multi-year fab timelines. AB.key_differentiator: Plan B front-loads the two things that actually kill this idea — decay/crowding (is it already priced and vendor-sold) and a simple LM regression that resolves the question in ten days — while Plan A buries the same question under a quarter of custom DeBERTa infrastructure that only matters if the effect survives the cheap test.
AB.rationale: Both plans are competent and both fit the systematic firm (peer-relative returns, cost/capacity/crowding as the failure modes, committee re-run). The decision turns on sequencing and edge. This is a heavily published question (Price et al. 2012, LM, and a decade of follow-on). The dominant risk is not measurement fidelity — it is that the effect is already arbitraged and sold as a vendor score. Plan B puts exactly that at the front: a day on McLean-Pontiff decay, vendor seat-cost/client-count calls as a direct crowding read, and a pre-registered gate with a hard kill (t of 2.1 kills it). It resolves the question with a plain LM tone regression the committee can trivially re-run in two weeks, and only builds the expensive DeBERTa/audio scope if the simple version passes. That is correct order and correct spend. Plan A is the more sophisticated study and its craft is real — point-in-time merges, timestamp audits, deflated Sharpe, an honest 'clean null is an output' — but it reaches for a domain-adapted transformer, 6k gold labels, 150k silver labels, and multi-head architecture before establishing that plain LM tone even survives orthogonalization against SUE/CAR/momentum. If the simple signal is dead-on-arrival (the a priori likely outcome given the literature), all that machinery was wasted, and its researcher degrees of freedom (many specifications, though it does pre-register one) inflate Type I. Plan A does address crowding as a break-even result, but it never asks the cheapest crowding question — does a vendor already sell this — which Plan B answers with a half-day of phone calls. On error asymmetry, this is a breadth signal over ~90k firm-quarters with capped per-name downside, so Type II matters, but the published-and-crowded prior makes an early, cheap kill the higher-value design regardless. Plan B's LM-first approach is also the simplest thing that could resolve it, and it explicitly defers LLM variants as exploratory precisely because of look-ahead contamination — a sharper handling of that risk than Plan A's rerun-with-earlier-cutoff. Plan B wins on order and cost discipline for a question where the answer is probably 'already priced.'
issues_with_winner: LM-only tone is a blunt measure; if the real signal lives in Q&A evasion or vocal/audio affect, Plan B may false-negative and log a kill on a signal that exists in a richer representation (it names this as the residual hypothesis, which mitigates but does not remove it)

BA.key_differentiator: Plan A puts the cheap idea-killing tests (crowding/vendor-availability check, decay prior, 2004-2010 replication, single pre-registered specification) up front and gates everything else behind them, while Plan B commits to a heavy multi-billion-token model build before establishing the effect exists.
BA.rationale: Both plans are written for exactly this firm — systematic, cost-and-crowding-aware, days-to-weeks horizon, committee that re-runs — and both correctly frame the question as a broad cross-sectional signal rather than a single name. AB.key_differentiator: Plan A holds the multiple denominator on realized LTM EBITDA to break the circularity the question is built on, while Plan B uses NTM EBITDA in the denominator and then tries to patch the resulting mechanical contamination with an accounting-identity decomposition — the cleaner measurement design wins for a fund that must defend this to a PM asking what would make it wrong.
AB.rationale: Both plans correctly read this as a broad cross-sectional effect question for a fundamental L/S fund with a data team but no ML/execution infra — both are firm-appropriate in horizon and infrastructure. The deciding issue is the circularity the question itself carries: forward multiples embed the revised estimate in the denominator, so a naive design finds the effect by construction. Plan A confronts this head-on as its framing premise and defends against it with a realized-LTM-EBITDA denominator (denominator not estimated), a feasibility gate (H0) that can kill the study in week one, and same-analyst-set revision measurement from detail files rather than the summary tape. Plan B acknowledges the same mechanical problem but keeps NTM EBITDA in the denominator and relies on an ex-post identity decomposition and 'report with/without Delta NTM EBITDA control' to disentangle it — a weaker fix that leaves the headline exposed to exactly the contamination the question warns about. Plan A also sequences the kill test first (H0 feasibility gate, then first-stage beta threshold with a stop), which is the right entropy-reducing order and gives the fund a cheap early exit. On economics, Plan B asserts specific elasticity magnitudes (8-12%/100bp, 2-5% measured) up front as anchors; Plan A derives beta* from realized persistence rather than importing a number. Plan A's main costs are real: it is heavy, imports a TAQ reverse-causality check the firm has no tick data to run (a firm-fit slip), and its regime-instability machinery (Bai-Perron, Kalman, variance ratios) is more than a 6-18mo fundamental shop can inspect or defend to a PM. Plan B is more restrained and its practical quintile-sort out-of-sample validation is exactly the judgeable output this fund can use. But measurement validity on the core circularity dominates: a cleaner-measured true effect beats a contaminated one wrapped in a good validation grid.
issues_with_winner: Proposes a TAQ tick-data reverse-causality check the firm explicitly lacks the infrastructure for
Regime-instability apparatus (Bai-Perron, Kalman filter, variance-ratio gating) exceeds what this fund can inspect or defend to a PM
Very long and dense; the decisive H0 gate is right but the surrounding machinery adds researcher degrees of freedom
Off-cycle event filter discarding 60-70% of events may leave thin samples in smaller industries
issues_with_loser: Keeps NTM EBITDA in the multiple denominator, reintroducing the exact circularity the question warns of, then only patches it via ex-post identity decomposition
Asserts specific theoretical elasticity magnitudes (8-12%/100bp) as up-front anchors before measuring anything
H4 industry-ranking hypothesis (software/semis vs utilities) risks fitting a story rather than testing the mechanism's absence conditions
No early feasibility/kill gate — every stage is scheduled regardless of whether the revision signal is even large enough to support inference

BA.key_differentiator: Plan A answers the question actually asked — do CAGR revisions drive peer-relative re-rating — with a design this firm can run and defend, while Plan B silently swaps the question for regime-instability and market-efficiency tests and reaches for infrastructure (TAQ, block bootstrap, Bai-Perron, Kalman) this fund cannot staff or evaluate.
BA.rationale: The question is whether next-two-year revenue and EBITDA CAGR revisions drive earnings-multiple re-rating among industry peers, for a fundamental L/S fund that will use the answer to size named positions over 6-18 months. Plan A takes this head on: it estimates the peer-relative elasticity, decomposes revenue vs EBITDA weight (H2), tests where it should be strongest by industry (H4), and anchors the measured elasticity against a DCF-implied theoretical value as a coherence check the PM can actually reason about. It confronts the one genuinely decisive threat — that DV and regressor share the EBITDA tape, so a whole-curve revision mechanically moves the multiple — and addresses it with an identity decomposition and by holding the denominator logic explicit. That is the right first-order concern and it is placed centrally. Plan B correctly flags the same circularity and its fix (LTM-fixed denominator, same-analyst revision filter) is genuinely elegant — better on that single measurement point than A. But B then abandons the asked question. Its two primary hypotheses are (H1) that the sensitivity is regime-unstable and (H2) that the market misprices the revision. Those are interesting but different questions; the fund asked whether the relationship exists and how it is weighted, not whether beta drifts across VIX terciles. B never cleanly delivers the base elasticity as a headline. On firm fit, B is written for a quant/event-study shop: single-broker event identification, TAQ reverse-causality checks, stationary block bootstrap with 10,000 reps, Bai-Perron sup-F, Kalman-filtered beta paths, 2SLS on fitted re-rating. This firm has one engineer, no tick data, and will not build production ML — they cannot run or defend most of this, and a PM asking 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong' cannot interrogate a Kalman beta path. A's methods (panel FE, clustered SEs, quintile sorts, placebo peer reassignment) are exactly what a three-person data team plus analysts can execute and a fundamental PM can follow. On simplest-thing-first, A starts with the elasticity and layers robustness; B front-loads a feasibility gate (good) but then buries the core relationship under machinery for second-order questions. Both name kill criteria and falsification tests. B's event-study rigor would win if the question were about pricing efficiency at a systematic shop — but it is not. A is the plan that answers this question for this firm.
issues_with_winner: Never fully resolves the shared-EBITDA-tape circularity — the identity decomposition mitigates but the headline still leans on Δlog EV which is not a clean re-rating measure
H1 elasticity magnitudes (2-5%/100bp) are asserted from DCF before measurement and risk anchoring interpretation
Heavy robustness grid adds researcher degrees of freedom; some branches (ex-2019, crisis exclusions, alt horizons) could be dropped or made conditional
Does not diff against sell-side consensus on whether this elasticity is already understood by the market — the edge question is underdeveloped
issues_with_loser: Reframes away from the asked question toward regime-instability and market-efficiency, answering something nobody asked
Method stack (TAQ, block bootstrap, Bai-Perron, Kalman, 2SLS) exceeds what this firm can staff, run, or defend to its PM
Off-cycle event restriction discards 60-70% of events, and single-broker revision events may be too sparse to power industry-level inference
Its cleaner denominator fix is real but does not compensate for solving a different problem than the one posed

AB.key_differentiator: Plan A puts the cheap decisive test ('is it already priced?') first and is built for a fundamental desk with no quant staff, while Plan B front-loads a Monte Carlo ramp-curve model this team cannot build, staff, or defend.
AB.rationale: The desk is a single-name event-driven team with one PM, two analysts, no quant research staff and no dataset-building capacity, consuming filings, sell-side and expert calls. The question is whether this specific situation is mispriced right now. Plan A matches that exactly: its gating stage one asks the entropy-reducing, idea-killing question first — how much of the check-driven optimism is already in consensus and price — and only proceeds to the guidance-mechanism work if a gap survives. That sequencing gets the desk to an actionable pass/proceed decision fast and cheaply, and killing the idea in stage one is treated as a valuable outcome. It also correctly diagnoses the edge question (checks are already public via sell-side, so what's left to earn) which is the crux for a mispricing call. Plan B answers a subtly different and harder question — a full bottom-up revenue reconstruction, least-squares-fit ramp curve R(k), and Monte Carlo over four parameters — which is capability this team lacks the staff to build or the vocabulary to defend to a fast-cutting risk manager. Plan B also invents economics: a 12% downside scenario, 50bps NAV risk budget, 4% NAV sizing and 8% stop asserted without the analysis producing them, and it buries its single most decisive finding (the backtest showing positive checks 6/8 but raises only 3/8 — the signal is uninformative, stop) in the middle of validation rather than at the front. That backtest alone should gate the whole effort and Plan A effectively runs the equivalent test early via its priced-in gate. Both plans understand the reflexivity/whisper point and both engage the disconfirming side. But Plan A is simpler, correctly sequenced, fits the firm, and puts the kill test first; Plan B is a systematic-shop plan dropped onto a fundamental desk.
issues_with_winner: The arithmetic-implied CAR back-out at constant multiple is itself a modeling step that could be argued over
Thresholds (0.5% consensus move, 1.2x straddle) are somewhat arbitrary and stated as if calibrated
Stage two still requires nontrivial guidance-history extraction that two analysts must do by hand
issues_with_loser: Monte Carlo ramp-curve fitting and bottom-up reconstruction exceed what a no-quant-staff fundamental desk can build, staff, or defend to an IC
Invents economics: 4% NAV sizing, 12% downside, 50bps risk budget, 8% stop asserted without derivation
Buries the decisive kill finding (6/8 checks positive, only 3/8 raises — signal uninformative) inside validation rather than running it first
Every stage is a prerequisite; cannot be stopped halfway and still have answered the mispricing question cheaply

BA.key_differentiator: Plan B puts the decisive kill test — is the channel-check thesis already in consensus and price — at the front, matching a firm with no quant staff, while Plan A leads with an elaborate bottom-up revenue reconstruction and Monte Carlo the desk cannot build or maintain.
BA.rationale: Both plans correctly read the goal: a single-name, weeks-to-months, is-this-mispriced-now question ahead of a specific print. The firm has one PM, two analysts, no quant staff, and consumes filings/sell-side/expert calls rather than building datasets. The decisive edge question here is that the channel checks are ALREADY public via sell-side notes — so the only thing that can pay is whether the optimism is already priced. Plan B leads with exactly that: a dated information-event log, consensus revision measurement, and an event study gate, with a pre-committed 'two of three fail and we stop' kill criterion up front. That is correct sequencing (kill test first), correct edge framing (diff against consensus/price), and it engages the other side (three of four outcome states are bad, default is no). Plan A does eventually check whether the market owns it, but only after a 12-quarter bottom-up revenue reconstruction, cohort ramp-curve least-squares fitting, and a Monte Carlo over four parameters — machinery this desk cannot build, staff, or defend to a fast-cutting risk manager, and which buries the decisive priced-in question. Plan A's guided-vs-actual backtest is a genuine strength (its own text shows the signal raises only 3/8 times — a real kill), but it is placed as validation after the heavy modeling rather than at the front. Plan B also handles the compliance/MNPI exposure of expert-network work, which Plan A ignores despite relying on 4-6 expert calls. Plan A's Sharpe-free but numerically specific outputs (75bps, 0.5x haircut, 4% NAV sizing) risk anchoring the desk on fabricated precision from an unmaintainable model. Type I dominates on a concentrated event-driven book with explicit downside, and Plan B's demanding, gated burden of proof fits that. Plan B wins on sequencing and firm fit; the margin is real but not overwhelming because Plan A contains the single best kill test.

Relies on precisely identifying an 'information date' for the check thesis, which may be fuzzy in practice
Stage-two guidance base rate over 12-16 quarters has a genuinely wide CI, as it admits — the conditional EV estimate may be weak
Assumes management policy is to hold/nudge without deep primary-source verification of the specific CFO's behavior
issues_with_loser: Bottom-up revenue reconstruction, ramp-curve least-squares fitting, and 4-parameter Monte Carlo require quant infrastructure and staff the desk explicitly does not have
Buries the decisive priced-in / signal-informativeness question behind heavy modeling — badly sequenced
Produces specific bps and NAV sizing figures that anchor on an unmaintainable model's precision
Ignores the MNPI/compliance exposure of its heavy expert-network reliance
Every stage is a prerequisite for the next; cannot be stopped halfway with a clean actionable answer as easily as B

AB.key_differentiator: Plan B puts the decisive question — does round-lot size actually mark retail flow — first with a cheap spreadsheet-only kill test, while Plan A builds the full signal machinery before confirming the premise the whole trade rests on.
AB.rationale: The question bundles two claims: that round lots identify retail, and that fading isolated retail flow pays after costs. Claim (1) is the load-bearing premise, and both analysts agree it is confounded by algo slicing and fractional/odd-lot retail migration. Plan B recognizes this and sequences for information: it runs a free Rule 605/FINRA wholesaler decomposition first (G-tests) that can kill the project in a week, uses venue partitioning to avoid pooling incommensurable flow, triangulates multiple imperfect retail labels with a latent-class estimator since no ground truth exists, and only builds the signal in a conditional Phase 2. Its evidence standard is judgeable (pre-committed lift/recall/signing thresholds) and it names a well-evidenced negative result plus a map of better identifiers as a valuable outcome. Plan A is technically excellent and does test the retail proxy via residualization rather than assuming it — but it interleaves the identification question with the full portfolio/cost/capacity build, so the expensive machinery runs regardless of whether the premise holds. It is a complete task list, not an adaptive plan; nothing is dropped based on intermediate results, and the decisive 'is this actually retail' question is answered alongside, not before, the harvestability question. For a 200-researcher systematic firm that can build either, the tiebreaker is which plan learns fastest and cheapest — that is B. Confidence is moderate because Plan A's cost/capacity/crowding treatment is genuinely superior on the harvestability half, and its residualization is a legitimate proxy validation; if the firm's real interest is a tradeable book rather than the mechanism, A's completeness has value B defers.
issues_with_winner: Phase 2 is sketched thinly — after-cost Sharpe and net/gross gates are stated but the impact model and capacity analysis are far less developed than A's
the ≥2x lift and ≥1/3 recall thresholds are asserted without derivation of why those magnitudes are the right bar
restricts to 36 months pre-half-penny, which limits the very regime-shift evidence about retail migration that motivates its own H0
RLP-flag historical feed availability is flagged as a risk but the whole G3 signing test depends on it existing
issues_with_loser: decisive identification question is not sequenced first — full portfolio, cost, and capacity machinery is committed before the retail-proxy premise is confirmed
non-adaptive: every stage runs regardless of intermediate results, no branch is dropped if RLOIB proves to be institutional slicing
no venue partitioning — pools all round-lot flow when the confound is precisely that different venues carry different origination
heavy researcher-degrees-of-freedom from the large sensitivity grid, harder to defend even at a sophisticated firm

BA.key_differentiator: Plan A puts the cheapest project-killing test (Rule 605 wholesaler buckets, spreadsheet-only) first and pre-commits a hard stop before any signal is built, decomposing the bundled question correctly; Plan B is a well-built but monolithic backtest whose every stage is a prerequisite for the next.
BA.rationale: Both plans correctly refuse to assume round lots mark retail — the shared, decisive insight given that retail migrated to fractional/dollar orders while schedulers slice into 100-share children. The question is which is better sequenced for information at a systematic firm that will independently re-run results. Plan A's central virtue is that it separates claim (1) 'round lots identify retail' from claim (2) 'trading against it pays' and gates the expensive Phase 2 signal build behind five identification tests, running the free Rule 605 / FINRA MPID check first because it alone can kill the project. That is entropy-reducing order and an adaptive, stoppable design — the most likely idea-killer is at the front, and a negative result plus a map of better retail identifiers is itself a valuable deliverable. Plan B is genuinely rigorous — Holden-Jacobsen cleaning, residualization against ALLOIB/ODDOIB/RETOIB, the STR-relabeling control, breakeven-cost-as-headline, capacity across AUM — all appropriate for this firm. But it is one large predictive-regression-plus-backtest that produces nothing judgeable until the whole pipeline runs; it never isolates the identification claim as a standalone gate. Its edge framing (crowding, capacity, STR contamination) actually fits the firm slightly better than A's, and its cost/capacity treatment is stronger. Both suit the audience's sophistication. I lean A because the decisive question here is measurement validity — does round-lot even mark retail post-migration — and A tests that cheaply and first, whereas B bundles it inside a $-heavy full study. This is close; A's Phase 2 is underspecified relative to B's cost work, which is why confidence is moderate.

Hui-Walter latent-class estimation may be more machinery than the research committee wants to re-run; A leans on it without a simple corroborating check the committee can eyeball

issues_with_loser: Monolithic design produces nothing a PM can act on until the full pipeline completes; not stoppable-halfway and not adaptive about which branch dies

AB.key_differentiator: The question is about one company that just guided, going to a skeptical IC at a concentrated long-only shop; Plan A builds a single-name forward-revenue bridge with an EV/consensus comparison, while Plan B builds a 20-30 episode cross-industry base-rate study answering 'do LTAs hold in general' — a different question for a different firm.
AB.rationale: The firm is a five-person fundamental long-only shop with no engineers, no database maintainer, and an IC skeptical of models it cannot inspect. The question is concrete and single-name: this company guided shortages, does that mean more durable revenue, and is it priced? Plan A answers exactly that. It builds a forward revenue bridge off this company's RPO/backlog/LTA disclosures, tiers commitments by structural quality, and — crucially — closes the loop against valuation via reverse DCF and EV/haircut-adjusted committed gross profit, so it produces a view on whether the market already prices the durability. That is where the edge is, and it is defensible to an IC because every step is inspectable in Bloomberg/Excel/filings. It also puts the decisive kill checks up front (negative implied gross bookings, definition changes, channel inventory) and engages the other side (enforcement rarely litigated, reflexivity, duration-vs-growth confusion). Plan B is a genuinely excellent piece of systematic research — but for a different firm. It requires Panjiva/ImportGenius customs data, PACER/Chancery/ICC legal mining, TrendForce/Fastmarkets/UxC/Drewry price series, and a 20-30 episode coded dataset with holdout validation. This shop cannot operate or maintain that, and the output is a general base rate about LTA durability across industries, not an answer about whether THIS name is mispriced. Plan B never diffs against this company's EV or consensus — it produces a probability-weighted haircut on a phenomenon, not an investment view on the position. For a concentrated book where being wrong about the business is the killer (Type I dominant), Plan A's demanding, name-specific, IC-defensible burden of proof is the right standard.
issues_with_winner: Very long and dense; the six-attribute scoring plus scenario paths plus reverse DCF is a lot for one analyst and risks researcher degrees of freedom
Some thresholds (90-95% Tier 1, 15% cash support, 2-year horizon gap) are asserted precision that could anchor without being well-calibrated from a single prior episode
Prior-cycle calibration leans on the same cross-episode history Plan B builds more rigorously, but does it more casually
issues_with_loser: Answers the general question (do shortage LTAs hold across industries) rather than the single-name question asked, and never connects to this company's valuation
Requires customs, legal-docket, and vendor price datasets plus a maintained coded episode database that a five-person shop with no data scientist cannot build or operate
Output is a base-rate haircut, not an actionable IC-defensible view on the specific position; wrong firm fit despite high quality

BA.rationale: The firm asked a single-name question: does this company's shortage guidance portend more durable revenue, and does the market already price it. Plan B answers exactly that. It stays on the actual company, rolls its RPO/backlog/LTA disclosures forward, scores the agreements by enforceability, compares EV against haircut-adjusted committed gross profit and a reverse DCF for the market-implied durable horizon — which directly engages the 'does consensus already hold this' edge question. Everything it uses (10-Ks, RPO footnotes, transcripts, customer mirror disclosures, Bloomberg) is executable by one analyst with no infrastructure, and the tiered haircut logic is exactly the kind of inspectable, defensible-to-a-skeptical-IC reasoning this shop needs. Its thresholds and negative triggers are concrete gut-checkable pass/fail conditions. Plan A is intellectually superior as a piece of research — the qualification-lag mechanism (contracts hold on volume, break on price, split by switching cost) is a genuine insight and its cross-episode base rates are rich — but it has misread the job. Assembling and coding 20-30 episodes across polysilicon, semis, memory, MLCC, substrates, uranium, LNG, containers, lithium, and aero forgings, with Panjiva/PACER/TrendForce/UxC/Argus data licences, is a multi-month research build this five-person shop cannot staff or maintain, and it produces a generalizable framework when the IC needs a verdict on one name. Plan A's output ('probability-weighted haircut') is close to what's wanted, but the path to it is a research project, not a single-analyst call. On error asymmetry both are demanding, which suits a concentrated book where being wrong about the business is the killer. B wins on goal match and firm fit — the two decisive tests.

issues_with_loser: Answers a broader question (does the LTA-durability effect exist across industries) than the one asked (this company, now)

Buries the decisive single-name test inside a large historical build; slow to produce something the PM can act on

AB.key_differentiator: The question is a single-name margin-risk call for a concentrated fundamental shop with no engineers, and Plan A answers exactly that while Plan B builds a 40,000-firm-quarter NLP panel nobody at the firm could operate or defend.
AB.rationale: The question is whether one company's vendor-licence renegotiation is a real near-term margin risk, for a five-person long-only shop on Bloomberg/Excel/filings with no data scientists and an IC skeptical of models it cannot inspect. Plan A matches both the goal and the firm precisely: it discards management tone as confounded (correctly — a CFO sounds guarded in any live negotiation), reframes to the answerable question of margin at stake, and sizes it from purchase-obligations tables, contract mechanics, vendor pricing behavior, and this pair's own renewal history. Every step is executable by one analyst in Bloomberg/Excel/filings, produces an inspectable sensitivity table the IC can interrogate, and back-tests against the prior renewal — a judgeable output for small N. Answers a broad panel question the single-name query never asked, and its own modal outcome is a null with no informational content
Produces nothing the skeptical IC can inspect or defend end to end
Slow to first actionable output; every stage is a prerequisite with no early single-name answer

BA.key_differentiator: The question is a single-name margin-risk assessment for a concentrated fundamental shop, and Plan B sizes the actual dollar exposure the firm can inspect and defend, while Plan A builds a 40,000 firm-quarter NLP panel that no one at this shop can operate, evaluate, or use.

Requires infrastructure, data science, and dataset licences this five-person shop explicitly cannot operate or maintain

Correctly notes contract topics are conditional and legal constraints mimic guilt, yet proceeds to build an enormous apparatus around a within-firm baseline that the case-specific facts would resolve faster

response.plan_implied_asker: a fundamental long/short fund testing a substitution mechanism to size DraftKings positions
response.what_would_falsify: Flat event-time coefficients beta_0..beta_6 (no post-adoption divergence in DraftKings deposit dollars), placebo/negative-control outcomes moving, or partial-identification breakdown M below ~1 — any of these means abandon the substitution claim.

issues.summary: The single most decisive check — does adopting Kalshi coincide with any drop in DraftKings spend at all — is buried behind a week of taxonomy work plus a full matching and stacked-DiD build.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A crude raw event-time plot of DraftKings deposit dollars around first Kalshi debit for eligible adopters can be produced in a day and would tell you whether there is any visible level shift to explain. If adopters show zero movement, the entire matching/PML/partial-ID apparatus is wasted. The plan schedules the parallel-trends plot inside Validation, after all machinery is built.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of taxonomy and matching effort are committed before the premise (any observable substitution) is confirmed to exist.
issues.fix: Run the unmatched adopter-vs-own-baseline event-time plot as step one, pre-registered as a go/no-go: no visible divergence in the raw series kills or pauses the build.

issues.summary: The plan does not test where substitution should be absent within the gambling category as a positive discriminator — its placebos are all non-gambling outcomes.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The mechanism is 'event contracts substitute for sportsbook wagering.' If Kalshi adoption reduces DraftKings AND FanDuel/BetMGM equally, that is category-wide gambling attrition (income shock, self-exclusion, life event), not Kalshi substitution. The FanDuel-only placebo pipeline tests the reverse, but held-out competitor spend among DraftKings adopters is used only as a balance covariate, not as an outcome that should move if substitution is real vs generic.
issues.what_breaks: A generic decline in all gambling spend gets attributed to Kalshi substitution, inflating the DraftKings-specific read.
issues.fix: Add competitor sportsbook spend (FanDuel/BetMGM/Caesars) as a co-outcome: substitution predicts DraftKings falls more than competitors among Kalshi adopters; parallel declines falsify the Kalshi-specific story.

issues.summary: No stated translation from panel deposit-dollar deltas to a DraftKings revenue/GGR impact, so the output cannot yet move position sizing as claimed.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Output is meant to change position sizing on DraftKings. A per-user deposit-dollar decline among Kalshi adopters is not a revenue impact without knowing Kalshi penetration of DraftKings' user base and the panel's representativeness of that base. The plan wisely avoids fabricating a number, but also never states the bridge needed to size the trade.
issues.what_breaks: The PM asks 'so how much does this move DraftKings revenue' and the study has no anchor; the result risks being over- or under-weighted in sizing.
issues.fix: Add a scoping step: estimate Kalshi adoption rate within the DraftKings-active panel and state explicitly that firm-level revenue impact = per-adopter effect x adoption share, flagged as the next deliverable rather than asserted.

response.overall: A genuinely strong, well-specified within-name causal design that fits the firm and the question, with a real falsifier, thoughtful placebos, and appropriate Type-I caution for a sizing decision. Two fixes matter: front-load the crude raw event-time check as a cheap go/no-go before building the matching apparatus, and add competitor-sportsbook spend as a co-outcome so Kalshi-specific substitution is distinguished from generic gambling attrition. The economics-to-sizing bridge is missing but is a next-step scoping gap, not a flaw in the causal work.

issue_buckets.why: Not in gold. A concrete, plan-specific sequencing objection: the raw event-time plot of DraftKings dollars around first Kalshi debit is cheap and is the premise test, yet the plan schedules it inside Validation after the full taxonomy/matching/stacked-DiD build. A desk with one engineer and a three-person data team would take the ordering point seriously.

Not in gold. Correctly reads the plan's own design: held-out FanDuel dollars appear only as a balance covariate, and the placebos are non-gambling categories plus a FanDuel-only-user pipeline. Treating competitor sportsbook spend as an outcome that should NOT fall if the mechanism is Kalshi-specific substitution is a legitimate discriminator against category-wide gambling attrition, and it is earned from this plan's specifics rather than recited.

Not in gold. Firm context explicitly requires output that changes position sizing on named companies and survives a PM's challenge; the plan stops at per-user deposit-dollar deltas with no stated bridge to DraftKings revenue/GGR via Kalshi penetration and panel representativeness. Specific to this plan's stated deliverable, not a generic complaint.

response.plan_implied_asker: a systematic panel-econometrics shop with an academic causal-inference bench
response.what_would_falsify: Permutation/mechanical null indistinguishable at 5%; placebos (grocery/streaming, non-legal states, neobank/P2P fake treatment) non-zero; six leads jointly significant; event-study ATT and regression β disagree beyond ~2x; out-of-sample 2024->2025 prediction fails.

issues.summary: The single cheapest test that could kill the whole idea — does Kalshi adoption coincide with a within-user DK drop at all — is buried behind an enormous estimation apparatus.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's first usable output arrives only after descriptor dictionary, PPML/asinh models, IV construction, Callaway-Sant'Anna, and power calcs. But a simple binned event-study plot of mean net DK funding in months t-6..t+6 around first Kalshi use, on the non-brokerage legal-state subsample, would show in days whether any displacement exists. If that plot is flat, everything downstream is wasted.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of analyst and engineer time are committed before the premise is shown to hold; a doomed idea takes months to kill instead of a week.
issues.fix: Front-load the raw within-user before/after mean plot with the mechanical-null overlay as step one, pre-committed as a gate: if no visible displacement survives the permuted null crudely, stop.

issues.summary: The methodological arsenal exceeds what a 30-person fundamental L/S PM can evaluate or defend, and much of it is redundant.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Driscoll-Kraay, wild bootstrap, ppmlhdfe, asinh, Arellano-Bond, IV with Kleibergen-Paap, Callaway-Sant'Anna, randomization inference — this is a publication-grade stack for a firm whose output is position sizing on named companies. The PM will ask 'what would have to be true for it to be wrong,' not whether the KP F-stat cleared 20. Most of these estimators answer the same question; three of them (donut event study, permutation null, placebos) carry the decision.
issues.what_breaks: The result becomes hard to defend internally precisely because no one on the desk can independently verify the machinery; researcher degrees of freedom multiply across a dozen specifications.
issues.fix: Lead with the within-user event study plus placebo panel — both directly inspectable — and relegate IV/Arellano-Bond to 'only if the simple result is marginal.' State which specifications are decision-relevant vs. robustness color.

issues.summary: The denominator/simultaneity problem is real and the plan's own primary regressor may not escape it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: H1's regressor is Kalshi share K/(K+DK+FD), which mechanically contains DK on both sides; a fall in DK raises share even with no behavioral substitution. The plan knows this (baseline-deflated K/W̄, permuted null) — but W̄ is a fixed pre-period mean, so a user whose total wallet shrinks for unrelated reasons still shows rising K/W̄ while DK falls. The permutation test guards mechanical reshuffling, not common wallet-shrinkage shocks.
issues.what_breaks: A significant β could reflect users cutting all discretionary spend (of which both Kalshi-funding and DK are part) rather than Kalshi displacing DK.
issues.fix: Lean on the wallet-accounting decomposition (does savings/discretionary rise as DK falls?) and the FD-symmetry contrast as the primary economic identification, not the share regression; treat the K/W̄ coefficient as corroborating.

issues.summary: Deposit-to-revenue conversion for DraftKings is asserted via take rates but the link to the equity thesis — what a displacement number means for DKNG earnings — is never built.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The panel covers a sliver of DK's user base; '$X displaced per 10-point share rise' on the panel does not extrapolate to a firmwide revenue delta without a panel-coverage/representativeness step the plan omits. The headline dollar figure risks being scaled into an implied DKNG revenue hit that the data cannot support.
issues.what_breaks: A PM could anchor position sizing on a panel-local number mistaken for a firmwide effect.
issues.fix: Add an explicit step estimating panel coverage as a share of DK's deposit base and state that the deliverable is the sign, magnitude-per-user, and concentration in high-value users — not a firmwide revenue forecast — unless coverage is validated.

issues.summary: The plan is largely a fixed pipeline; it states kill criteria but not which branches drop when.
issues.why_it_applies_here: It pre-commits pass/fail thresholds (good) but runs pooled-plus-ten-splits, IV, event study and Arellano-Bond regardless of whether the headline effect is obvious or null. If the raw event study shows a clean strong effect, the IV and dynamic-panel work are unnecessary; if it shows nothing, the cuts are pointless.
issues.what_breaks: Effort is spent symmetrically across a decision tree that early results should prune.
issues.fix: Add explicit branching: 'if event study + placebos pass cleanly and effect is large, skip IV; if marginal, run IV; if null on the gate, stop.'

response.overall: The econometrics is genuinely strong — the mechanical-null, placebo battery, wallet-accounting, and out-of-sample gate are exactly the right falsifiers, and the plan takes the denominator and attribution problems seriously. The two real problems are ordering and calibration: the single cheap test that could kill the idea is buried behind a research-grade estimation stack that this fundamental desk cannot fully evaluate or defend, and the pipeline runs symmetrically rather than pruning on early results. Reorder to front-load the raw within-user event study plus placebos as a gate, designate three decision-relevant tests versus robustness color, and ensure the deliverable stays at 'sign, per-user magnitude, and concentration in high-value users' rather than a firmwide revenue number the panel coverage cannot yet support.

issue_buckets.why: Same concern as blocking#1: the existence/direction question can be answered with a simple within-user event study, and the plan's regression-first apparatus displaces the cheap decisive test. Concretely grounded in the plan's own subsamples (non-brokerage, legal states, t-6..t+6).

Substantially the same complaint as blocking#1's 'spends its design budget' point — the estimator stack is publication-grade for a desk whose deliverable is position sizing, and the reviewer's implication is that the decision rests on a few simple checks. Overlap is close enough to call matched, though it is framed as complexity/defensibility rather than wrong-tool, hence flagged uncertain.

Directly the denominator/simultaneity problem named in blocking#1, and it goes further by showing the plan's stated fix is incomplete: fixed W\u0304 leaves rising K/W\u0304 with falling DK under a common wallet-shrinkage shock, which the within-user permutation null does not cover. Engaged with the plan's specific defences rather than recited.

Not in gold but a legitimate desk-level gap: the plan converts deposits to revenue via take rates yet never builds the panel-coverage/representativeness bridge from a panel-local '$ displaced per 10-point share rise' to a DKNG revenue delta, which is exactly the number a PM would size on. Specific to this plan's headline metric, not a generic alt-data caveat.

Legitimate and grounded in named plan components (pooled-plus-ten-splits, IV, Arellano-Bond run regardless of the headline result): kill criteria are pre-set but no branch-pruning logic is specified. Risks being partly a restatement of [0]/[1] on effort allocation, so flagged uncertain.

response.plan_implied_asker: a fundamental L/S fund with an alt-data panel team and 6-18 month horizon
response.what_would_falsify: Refit on excluded consumption-priced names; equal performance sinks the thesis. Also: MAU fails to beat two-way FE benchmark C out-of-sample under Diebold-Mariano p<0.05.

issues.summary: The deliverable predicts ARR (the fundamental), but the fund trades named stocks on a 6-18mo horizon, and the plan never tests whether the MAU-to-ARR signal is incremental to consensus at print.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The output is meant to change position sizing on named companies. Predicting ARR accurately is worthless if consensus already prices it — and the plan captures Visible Alpha consensus but only uses it as a dispersion yardstick, never as the thing to beat. The benchmark set (carry-forward, trailing growth, FE-without-MAU) is mechanical, not the market. Getting ARR right and the stock not moving is the exact failure mode this fund's PM will ask about.
issues.what_breaks: The validation step declares victory when MAU beats naive extrapolation C, but a signal can beat C and still be fully priced by sell-side. The 'edge' is asserted as better measurement but never diffed against consensus expectations.
issues.fix: Add a step: does the MAU-implied ARR surprise predict the actual ARR surprise versus Visible Alpha consensus, and does the residual predict post-print stock returns over the trading horizon? That is the investable question. Beating C is table stakes, not the deliverable.

issues.summary: The falsifier (refit on consumption-priced names) is a good negative control but is scheduled at the very end, behind the entire estimation and validation apparatus.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The consumption-names control is cheap and could invalidate the mechanism story early — if MAU 'predicts' revenue equally well for Snowflake, the signal is measuring something generic (size, growth momentum) not seat billing. Running it last means the expensive machinery is built before the premise is stress-tested.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of panel construction and econometrics are sunk before the one test that could show the mechanism is illusory. Front-loading it would prune a doomed branch cheaply.
issues.fix: Move the consumption-names negative control forward: fit the simple within-company log-log regression on both seat and consumption names first. If MAU tracks revenue equally in both, stop.

issues.summary: MAU is an unvalidated proxy for seats; the mechanism requires MAU-per-seat and price-per-seat to drift slowly, but the plan asserts this rather than measuring it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Named companies disclose seat/customer counts and net revenue retention. The plan controls for price drift via Wayback snapshots but never checks the core link: does MAU actually move with billed seats within a company, or with engagement per seat (which is decorrelated from billing)? Shelfware — paid seats not logging in — is exactly the case where MAU and ARR diverge, and it is handled only as an asymmetry interaction after the fact.
issues.what_breaks: If MAU-per-seat is not slow-moving, β is unstable and the whole 1%-MAU-implies-β%-ARR framing is measuring engagement, not billing. The signal would work in expansion and fail in the flat/decline regimes that matter most for shorts.
issues.fix: Where disclosed, regress MAU on reported seats/customers directly for a subset of names to validate the proxy-to-target link before assuming it. Report the MAU/seat ratio time series.

issues.summary: ~40 effective clusters and 35-60 names with heterogeneous business models is thin for the pooled panel econometrics stacked on top.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan itself flags ~40 effective clusters, then applies CIPS, Westerlund, ECM, Driscoll-Kraay, wild cluster bootstrap, Pesaran CD. Wild cluster bootstrap and CD tests are near their reliability floor at 40 clusters. The real evidence here is within-name consistency over quarters, which the rolling-origin and LOCO checks capture well — the panel-cointegration layer adds researcher degrees of freedom without adding conviction the PM can use.
issues.what_breaks: The sophisticated panel tests will produce numbers that look authoritative but are underpowered at this N, and the PM cannot defend them. The credible evidence is the per-name trend-tracking, which the simpler benchmarks and rolling-origin already deliver.
issues.fix: Lead with the simple within-name check and rolling-origin MAPE; keep the panel unit-root/cointegration battery as an appendix robustness note, not a gate. The corroborating simple check the audience can verify is already present — make it the headline.

response.overall: This is a well-constructed, genuinely rigorous plan that correctly matches the firm's horizon, infrastructure and defensibility needs, and it engages falsification seriously with a real negative control. The blocking gap is target substitution: it predicts ARR accurately but never tests whether that prediction is incremental to sell-side consensus or translates into stock moves the fund can trade — beating a naive carry-forward is not the same as an edge. Fix by making the consensus-surprise-to-return link the deliverable, validate MAU-against-disclosed-seats before assuming the proxy, and move the cheap consumption-names control to the front.

issue_buckets.why: Not in gold, but a sharp, plan-specific point: the plan licenses Visible Alpha consensus point items (subscription revenue, ARR, NRR, billings) at print morning yet only ever uses consensus as a dispersion yardstick, never as the benchmark to beat. Benchmarks A/B/C are all mechanical extrapolations. Given the mandate (change position sizing on named names, defend to a PM), incrementality to the priced expectation is a legitimate desk-level objection and is earned from the plan's own text rather than recited generically.

Legitimate and specific to this plan's ordering: the consumption-priced-names falsifier (Snowflake, Datadog, etc.) is cheap, could kill the seat-billing mechanism outright, and is placed after the full estimation/validation build. Sequencing critique that a desk with three data staff and one engineer would take seriously; not a canonical recitation.

Engages the plan's own stated mechanism condition ('MAU is not seats; the mechanism needs MAU-per-seat and price per seat drifting slowly') and notes the plan never measures it despite disclosed seat/customer counts and NRR being available for these named issuers, and despite shelfware being handled only as a post-hoc asymmetry interaction. That is a concrete gap, not a generic proxy-validity complaint, and it bears directly on short-side reliability at this horizon.

Borders on the canonical sample-size objection, but it is at least partly earned: it quotes the plan's own ~40 effective clusters and argues the CIPS/Westerlund/ECM/CD layer adds researcher degrees of freedom the PM cannot defend. The specific claim that wild cluster bootstrap is 'near its reliability floor' at 40 clusters is shaky — that bootstrap is precisely the recommended fix for few clusters — which weakens the technical basis. Kept as real_unlisted because the broader 'too much machinery for this N, the credible evidence is within-name consistency' point is a legitimate desk objection; flagged uncertain given the mis-stated statistical premise.

response.plan_implied_asker: a fundamental L/S fund with an alt-data panel team wanting a defensible nowcast across a small set of seat-based SaaS names
response.what_would_falsify: Gate failure: β̂ not positive/significant at 5% under block bootstrap, or β̂ outside [0.5,1.5], or within-company partial correlation <0.45, or unstable across halves/leave-one-out — any of which yields a documented negative result rather than a fallback.

issues.summary: The deliverable nowcasts ARR growth, but the fund's output is position sizing — and the plan never connects the ARR nowcast to stock outperformance or to what consensus already expects.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm sizes named positions on a 6–18mo horizon; being right about ARR is only investable if the ARR view differs from what is already priced. The plan's only nod to consensus is a surprise-space regression at the end (model-minus-consensus), which is the right instinct but is buried as a validation add-on, not the gating question. A perfectly calibrated seat nowcast that agrees with sell-side estimates changes no position.
issues.what_breaks: Even a fully passing gate and nowcast could produce zero edge if the panel MAU signal is already embedded in consensus (these are heavily-covered names with the same alt-data vendors sold to everyone). The whole pipeline can succeed on its own terms and still not move sizing.
issues.fix: Promote the model-minus-consensus surprise test to a co-primary gate: does the MAU-derived ARR nowcast systematically anticipate consensus revisions and, ideally, post-print drift on these names? Kill early if the signal is coincident with, not ahead of, consensus.

issues.summary: Panel MAU on authenticated post-login paths is a weak proxy for billable seats precisely where the money is — enterprise SaaS with managed devices, SSO, VPN and desktop clients.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's own pitfalls list 'enterprise blindness' as the dominant failure mode, then relegates it to a coverage-trend warning and a second vendor. For Atlassian, Smartsheet, monday, the seats that matter most are exactly the ones panels see least (corporate networks, thick clients). Coverage isn't just noisy — it is systematically biased against the highest-value cohort, and that bias can trend with product/deployment mix.
issues.what_breaks: The gate regression β could pass on the visible slice while the invisible slice drives actual ARR growth, giving a signal that works in backtest on disclosers and fails on the names you'd actually trade. The coverage-drift kill (>10%/yr) may not catch a stable-but-biased coverage floor.
issues.fix: Make coverage adequacy a first, cheap gate before any modeling: for the seat-like disclosers, plot panel-MAU/disclosed-seats level and its stability per company. If coverage is <~a few percent or the level is unstable for the enterprise names, kill those names up front rather than modeling them.

issues.summary: Contemporaneous nowcasting of a quantity most companies disclose within weeks offers little on a 6–18 month horizon.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The primary claim is a contemporaneous proxy; the nowcast fires five business days after quarter end. The fund holds 6–18 months. A nowcast of a number reported ~4–6 weeks later is only valuable if it (a) beats consensus ahead of the print or (b) predicts the trajectory several quarters out. The lead-quarter diagnostic is the valuable piece and is treated as secondary ('a lead becomes the nowcast core' only if it appears).
issues.what_breaks: If the signal is only contemporaneous and not leading, the informational value decays to near zero for this horizon — you learn the ARR growth a few weeks before it's disclosed, which rarely justifies a sizing change held for a year.
issues.fix: Elevate the leading-indicator test to primary. Gate on whether MAU growth predicts ARR growth one-to-two quarters ahead, not just contemporaneously; a contemporaneous-only result should be treated as a marginal outcome, not success.

issues.summary: The sample is a handful of seat-disclosing names, several of which are not the names to be traded, and cross-sectional generalization is thin.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The gate is validated on seat-like disclosers (ADP, Paycom, Dayforce, Dropbox, etc.), but the tradable universe is the seat-based SaaS names that don't cleanly disclose seats — that is the whole point of building the proxy. Success on disclosers is the correct calibration approach, but the plan should be explicit that it is generalizing from where seats ARE disclosed to where they are NOT, and that this leap is untested.
issues.what_breaks: β estimated on ADP/Paycom (payroll, near-perfect seat visibility) may not transfer to Asana/monday (fuzzy free tiers, deskless users). The two-thirds-of-firms consistency check partly guards this but pooling heterogeneous business models risks a mechanical average that fits no single tradable name.
issues.fix: State the generalization explicitly and add a per-company consistency-over-time judgement for the actual target names, rather than leaning on pooled significance. Treat the disclosers as a training/validation set and the target names as held-out, judged on trend agreement where any partial disclosure exists.

issues.summary: Ridge + nested CV + empirical-Bayes shrinkage is more machinery than the small-N problem needs and harder to defend to the PM.
issues.why_it_applies_here: With a dozen-ish companies and a lagged-dependent-variable nowcast, the simple pooled FE regression plus damped AR(1) baseline already resolves most of the question. The ridge/EB layer adds researcher degrees of freedom the pitfalls section then has to police (specification count). The plan does pair it with a simple baseline, which mitigates — but the marginal value over a shrunk pooled OLS is unlikely to survive OOS on N this small.
issues.what_breaks: Extra tuning surface invites overfit on tiny folds and gives the PM a harder-to-explain model without materially better forecasts.
issues.fix: Run the simple pooled FE + damped-AR(1) nowcast first as the deliverable; only add ridge/EB if the simple version demonstrably underperforms on walk-forward, and report the delta.

response.overall: Methodologically careful, well-firm-fit, and unusually good at pre-committing kill criteria and falsifiers — this is a competent proxy-calibration plan. But it answers the wrong end of the question for this fund: it nowcasts ARR growth without establishing that the ARR view is (a) ahead of consensus and (b) tradable on a 6–18mo horizon, and it under-weights that panel coverage is structurally blind to exactly the enterprise seats that drive ARR. Promote the consensus-surprise and leading-indicator tests to primary gates, front-load a cheap coverage-adequacy screen, and trim the ridge/EB layer until the simple version fails.

issue_buckets.why: Not in gold. Legitimate and firm-specific: output is position sizing on named companies, so an accurate ARR nowcast that matches consensus moves nothing, and these vendors' panels are sold widely. The plan does carry a pre-print consensus baseline and a surprise-space regression, which the evaluator concedes, so the point is about ordering/gating rather than absence — but a desk would still take seriously the demand that beating consensus be the gate rather than a validation appendix.

Not in gold, and earned on this plan's specifics rather than recited. It engages the plan's own machinery — that enterprise blindness is listed as the dominant failure mode yet handled only by a coverage-trend kill (>10%/yr drift) and a second vendor — and makes the sharper point that a stable-but-biased coverage floor passes that kill while the invisible high-value cohort drives ARR. Names the affected companies (Atlassian, Smartsheet, monday). A desk would take this.

Not in gold. Tied concretely to the firm context (6–18 month horizon) and to the plan's own design choice (contemporaneous claim, nowcast five business days after quarter end, lead quarter demoted to a diagnostic). The objection that learning a number a few weeks before it is disclosed rarely justifies a year-long sizing change is specific and defensible, not a generic horizon complaint.

This is the objection the reviewer explicitly ruled out. The reviewer wrote that the thinness of the seat-disclosing gate sample is not an objection because the output is per-name and an analysis working on one or two relevant companies is fine if defensible on those names. Issue [3]'s core complaint is exactly that the sample is 'a handful of seat-disclosing names' with 'thin' cross-sectional generalization and that the calibration names are not the tradable names — i.e. it demands the cross-sectional breadth the reviewer said is unnecessary given per-name output.

Not in gold. Reads as a canonical-overfitting theme but is actually earned here: it points at the specific machinery in this plan (ridge with nested CV plus empirical-Bayes shrinkage on roughly a dozen companies), ties it to the firm's stated constraint of not building production ML and needing to defend to a PM, and even acknowledges the mitigating damped-AR(1) baseline. Legitimate desk-level concern about researcher degrees of freedom relative to marginal forecast gain.

response.plan_implied_asker: an alt-data L/S fund needing a defensible ID-to-ticker matching layer before it can trade the panel
response.what_would_falsify: Null (permuted-customer) silhouette unbeaten, bootstrap Jaccard <0.6, or cross-window ARI <0.4 — any of these forces reporting only country/business-model separation and refusing named matches.

issues.summary: The plan runs the full clustering/naming/validation pipeline before establishing whether any named match can be verified against ground truth the desk trusts.
issues.why_it_applies_here: What kills the work is a confident wrong match. The entire validation ladder tests internal cohesion and stability (silhouette, Jaccard, ARI, permutation null) — none of which establishes correctness of a name. A cluster can be sharply separated, stable, and beat the null while being mapped to the wrong bank, because the Hungarian assignment rests on rank-agreement between panel-customer counts and market share, which is a plausibility heuristic, not a verification.
issues.what_breaks: The 'named institution' tier (B/C) is the only output the desk can trade on, and it arrives at the very end resting on an unverified assumption. The PM's question — what would have to be true for this to be wrong — is not answered by any stated step, because no independent external check of a name is ever performed.
issues.fix: Front-load a ground-truth anchor set: identify a handful of IDs whose bank is knowable with near-certainty from an external tell (a bank-specific domestic scheme monopoly, a unique product, a regulatory quirk, a merchant/counterparty ID that only one institution issues) and confirm the pipeline recovers them before building the rest. If even a handful cannot be independently confirmed, the naming tier is undeliverable and the project stops at archetype.

issues.summary: The named-match decision rule (rank agreement plus a margin) has no stated false-match rate and no external calibration of what the margin buys.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Given Type I dominance here — a wrong name means sizing on another bank's customers — the naming gate needs a quantified error rate, not a 'preset margin' and '≤3 candidates.' The plan never says how often the constrained-assignment step would name the wrong institution when tested against known cases, so the PM cannot judge whether Tier B is safe to trade.
issues.what_breaks: Constrained-assignment naming step: the accept threshold is asserted, not calibrated. Downstream, the desk cannot distinguish a defensible named match from a lucky rank coincidence in a concentrated country-archetype cell where two banks have similar share.
issues.fix: Using the anchor set above, measure the empirical wrong-name rate of the assignment rule at candidate margins and set the accept threshold to a false-match rate the desk pre-commits to (e.g. name only when demonstrably below X%). Report the confusion cases.

issues.summary: The plan is over-scoped for what is, at core, a matching-feasibility question that could be triaged far more cheaply.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Three clustering algorithms, co-association reconciliation, NMF co-holding loadings, PageRank, GMM full-covariance, UMAP, and a 500-iteration Hennig bootstrap are all committed up front. But the binding question — can an anonymized ID be tied to a specific bank with acceptable error — may be answerable for the easy cases (country-monopoly domestic schemes, unique counterparty IDs, dominant incumbents) with simple deterministic tells, and impossible for the hard cases regardless of clustering sophistication. The 3-person data team and one engineer can operate this, but much of it may be wasted motion.
issues.what_breaks: Weeks of pipeline construction precede any evidence that named matching is achievable, committing analyst time before the cheap version has shown the idea works.
issues.fix: First pass: attempt deterministic identification via unique institutional tells (scheme issuance, unique counterparty/BIN signatures, single-bank products) on the highest-share IDs. This alone may resolve the tradeable names. Reserve the clustering machinery for the residual and for archetype-only tiers where deterministic tells fail.

issues.summary: Country/archetype separation is confirmatory of what is already knowable, not incremental — only the named tier is potentially investable.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The desk wants to underwrite specific listed banks. Knowing an ID is 'a German savings-specialist' is not attachable to a ticker and adds nothing over public market-structure data. The edge exists only if the named tier clears, so the plan's value is entirely contingent on the naming step the validation does not verify.
issues.what_breaks: If naming fails, the deliverable collapses to a restatement of ECB/EBA market structure the fund already has, with no tradeable output despite full pipeline cost.
issues.fix: State explicitly that archetype-only is a negative result for this fund's purpose, and gate continued spend on the naming feasibility check succeeding first.

response.overall: This is a technically strong, self-aware capability build — the pitfalls section anticipates account-role confounding, panel skew, and aggregator/white-label IDs, and the negative-result path is honestly pre-committed. But it is misordered for the one thing that kills the work: the entire validation ladder proves cohesion and stability, never correctness of a name, and the confident-wrong-match risk lives entirely in an uncalibrated rank-assignment rule that arrives last. Before building the pipeline, establish an external ground-truth anchor set and measure the false-name rate of the assignment rule; if a handful of names cannot be independently confirmed cheaply, the tradeable tier is undeliverable and that should be established in week one, not month three.

issue_buckets.why: Same concern as gold blocking#2 (gates test stability, not correctness; no external ground truth ever brought to bear) and overlaps blocking#1 (rank-agreement naming is a heuristic, not evidence). Framed as sequencing but the substance is the reviewer's objection.

Attacks the same constrained-assignment naming rule as gold blocking#1 — the accept margin and '\u22643 candidates' are asserted, with no false-match rate and no external calibration. This is the reviewer's 'not the evidence-based identification this task needs' point expressed as a missing quantified Type I rate, and ties to blocking#2's lack of external truth.

Not in the gold, but a legitimate desk objection specific to this plan: the plan commits three clusterers, co-association reconciliation, NMF, PageRank, GMM, UMAP and a 500-iteration Hennig bootstrap before testing the binding feasibility question, when the panel actually contains cheap deterministic tells (two-legged-transfer counterparty institution IDs, domestic-scheme membership, unique merchant/counterparty IDs) that could triage easy named cases first. The critique is earned from this plan's own data fields and its 3-person team, not recited generically.

The reviewer explicitly ruled this out in anti_objection#3: an unidentifiable but stable cluster is a Type II miss, and the tiering is judged to handle it correctly by leaving IDs at country+archetype rather than forcing a name. Issue [3] recasts precisely that fallback as a defect ('collapses to a restatement of ECB/EBA market structure', 'no tradeable output'), i.e. treats the reviewer's accepted Type II outcome as a failure the reviewer had already considered and dismissed.

response.plan_implied_asker: an alt-data-mature systematic-leaning L/S fund that treats a confident wrong match as the killing risk
response.what_would_falsify: Below 40% of panel deposit volume assignable at \u226595% precision on held-out institutions a country is declared not identifiable; permuted fingerprints must score at chance and phantom IDs must abstain.

issues.summary: The matching machinery (min-cost flow, Jonker\u2013Volgenant, Sinkhorn marginals, Venn\u2013Abers/split-conformal, Wasserstein/JS scoring) is not defensible to the PM who must ask 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong.'
